lawyer: Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, Deputy Attorney-General, AFM Shahed, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Petitioner
parties:
Bangladesh ------ Petitioner
vs.
Sessions Judge and Special Tribunal No. 1 Chittagong and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Therefore, it appears to us that where there is efficacious remedy provided by law Article 102 is not attracted. The judgment and order sought to be declared as have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect is appealable under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. But the petitioner, the State, has not taken appeal to the High Court Division from the said judgment and order within the prescribed period of limitation of 30 days contemplated under section 30 of the Act. 

 3. The learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that as no appeal was filed under section 30 of the Act and as section 5 of the Limitation Act is not made applicable for condonation of delay for filing appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 the petitioner has no other efficacious remedy other than the one available under Article 102 of the Constitution. The submission is misconceived simply on the ground that the Special Tribunal in passing the judgment and the order has acted with lawful authority and the same does not suffer for want of authority. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also could not show us anything that the Special Tribunal acted without lawful authority. The learned Deputy Attorney General, however, made a submission that because of the decision in the case of Mir Mohammad Ali and Md. Giasuddin vs State 46 DLR 175, writ lies. Shortly we will examine the decision. Special Tribunal is a creature of Special Powers Act, 1974, a special enactment, which provides a special machinery for dealing with the offences mentioned therein. The parliament also consciously did not make section 5 of the Limitation Act available for condonation of delay in filing an appeal from the judgment and order of the Special Tribunal. Thus, when parliament in a subsequent enactment omitted application of section 5 of the Limitation Act, the petitioner, who is the State should not be allowed to invoke in a circuitous way the high prerogative discretionary jurisdiction of Article 102 of the Constitution. The learned Deputy Attorney-General referred to us paragraph 13 of the said decision to argue that from the judgment and order writ jurisdiction is available. Paragraph 13 is: 

 "Mr. Paul, on the other hand, has submitted that when appeals have been barred by limitation the accused, who have been convicted under the Special Powers Act, may not be, when their appeal is time barred, without any relief in appropriate cases, viz, when the trial is without jurisdiction or when the conclusion is absurd in view of evidence, They might seek relief under Article 102 (2) (ii) of the Constitution in such cases. If it transpired that the Court concerned had no jurisdiction to proceed with the case or the jurisdiction of the court has been exercised in an absurd or preposterous way, the accused might have recourse to the constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court".
